title: #68 Make Groups Explicitly Random and Change Them Regularly
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Drawing on Peter Liljedahl's Building Thinking Classrooms, Barton shares three group-work recommendations beyond his earlier tip about using groups of three rather than four. Changing groups regularly (Liljedahl suggests every lesson) prevents students from settling into fixed roles, where one or two students consistently lead the thinking while others become passive "passengers." Making group allocation genuinely random removes the self-fulfilling narrative students construct about why they were grouped a certain way. And making that randomness visibly explicit matters as much as the randomness itself, since students are unlikely to trust a claimed-random allocation unless they see the mechanism -- Liljedahl suggests students draw a card on entry and sit at the matching table, though Barton notes a random-name generator on the board works just as well. Barton is candid that he didn't agree with everything in the book, but treats these three specific recommendations as a useful, evidence-informed starting point for getting group-work structure right.
points: Static groups let students settle into fixed roles -- a few "lead the thinking" while others become passive "passengers" -- a dynamic that regular reshuffling (ideally every lesson, per Liljedahl) disrupts.
Genuine randomness in group allocation removes the ability-signalling narrative students otherwise construct about why they were placed together.
Randomness has to be visibly demonstrated, not just asserted -- students who don't see the allocation mechanism are unlikely to believe the grouping was actually random.
Barton frames these three practices as a starting point, not a complete solution, explicitly flagging that effective group work involves more than allocation alone.
quotes: If groups remain consistent over time, students are likely to fall into certain roles within a group. One or two students always lead the thinking, while other students in the group adopt the role of passengers.
Changing the groups regularly—Liljedahl recommends doing this every lesson - means each group provides an opportunity to start afresh.
Students always have a suspicion as to why they have been put into a particular group - oh, I am not as smart as those guys, so my job is to be a passenger.
Even if you genuinely do randomly allocate the groups, students are unlikely to believe it is random. So, they need showing.
Liljedahl recommends asking students to pick a card from a deck upon entry to the classroom and then sit on the table corresponding to the number on their card.
Of course, allocating the groups is just the tip of the iceberg in terms of getting group work right, but thinking about it is an interesting place to start.
